title: Sophie Germain Prime Counting Function
content: Defines $\pi_{SG}(n)$ as the cardinality of Sophie Germain primes in $\{0, 1, \ldots, n\}$. Uses `Finset.range(n+1)` to generate candidates, `filter` with the `IsSophieGermainPrime` predicate, and `.card` to count. Declared `noncomputable` because `IsSophieGermainPrime` involves `Decidable` instances that are not computationally available in general.
mathContext: $\pi_{SG}(n) = |\{p \in \{0, \ldots, n\} : \text{IsSophieGermainPrime}(p)\}|$. In Lean: `(Finset.range (n+1)).filter (fun p => IsSophieGermainPrime p) |>.card`.

title: Sophie Germain Primes Are a Subset of All Primes
content: Every Sophie Germain prime is a prime (the condition adds the requirement that $2p+1$ also be prime). Therefore $\pi_{SG}(n) \leq \pi(n)$. The proof uses `Finset.card_le_card` to reduce to showing that the SG-prime filter is a subset of the prime filter, which follows from destructuring `IsSophieGermainPrime` to extract the underlying primality.
mathContext: $\pi_{SG}(n) \leq \pi(n)$ since $\{p \leq n : \text{SG prime}\} \subseteq \{p \leq n : \text{prime}\}$. The proof extracts `hp.1 : Nat.Prime p` from `hp : IsSophieGermainPrime p`.

title: Monotonicity of the Counting Function
content: If $m \leq n$, then $\pi_{SG}(m) \leq \pi_{SG}(n)$. This is an essential property for any counting function. The proof shows the filtered finset for $m$ is a subset of that for $n$: any $p$ in $\{0, \ldots, m\}$ that is an SG prime is also in $\{0, \ldots, n\}$ (since $p \leq m \leq n$), and `omega` handles the arithmetic.
mathContext: $m \leq n \Rightarrow \pi_{SG}(m) \leq \pi_{SG}(n)$. Monotonicity makes $\pi_{SG}$ a valid counting function in the analytic number theory sense.
relatedConcepts: counting functions in analytic number theory

title: Computing Concrete Values
content: Three concrete computations: $\pi_{SG}(0) = 0$, $\pi_{SG}(1) = 0$, $\pi_{SG}(2) = 1$. The first two use `interval_cases` to enumerate all $p \leq 0$ (resp. $\leq 1$) and check none satisfies `IsSophieGermainPrime`. The third uses `decide` to evaluate the finite computation directly: 2 is the smallest Sophie Germain prime since both 2 and $2 \cdot 2 + 1 = 5$ are prime.
mathContext: The Sophie Germain primes begin: $2, 3, 5, 11, 23, 29, 41, 53, 83, 89, \ldots$ The first SG prime is 2: both 2 and $2(2)+1 = 5$ are prime. The Lean `decide` tactic evaluates $\pi_{SG}(2) = 1$ by brute-force computation on $\{0, 1, 2\}$.

title: The Twin Prime Constant
content: Defines $C_2 \approx 0.6602$ as a noncomputable real number. The true value is the infinite product $C_2 = \prod_{p \geq 3 \text{ prime}} p(p-2)/(p-1)^2$, but this is approximated here to avoid axiomatizing the existence of infinite products. This design keeps the entry at 0 axioms -- the constant is stated as a definition, not an assumption.
mathContext: $C_2 = \prod_{p \geq 3} \frac{p(p-2)}{(p-1)^2} = \prod_{p \geq 3} \left(1 - \frac{1}{(p-1)^2}\right) \approx 0.6601618158\ldots$ The constant appears in the asymptotics of both twin primes and Sophie Germain primes because both involve pairs of primes separated by a fixed linear function.

title: Residue Class Constraint: p ≡ 2 (mod 3)
content: For Sophie Germain primes $p > 3$: $p \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$. The proof eliminates $p \equiv 0$ (since $p$ is prime and $p > 3$, so $3 \nmid p$) and $p \equiv 1$ (since $2(1) + 1 = 3 \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$, giving $3 \mid (2p+1)$, contradicting primality of $2p+1 > 3$). This is the **simplest sieve condition** for Sophie Germain primes: it eliminates all primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$.
mathContext: If $p \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$, then $2p + 1 \equiv 2(1) + 1 = 3 \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$, so $3 \mid (2p+1)$. Since $p > 3$ implies $2p+1 > 7 > 3$, the number $2p+1$ is divisible by 3 but not equal to 3, contradicting primality. Therefore $p \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$.

title: Residue Class Constraint: p ≡ 5 (mod 6)
content: Strengthens the mod 3 result: for $p > 3$, combining $p \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$ with $p$ odd (since $p > 2$ and prime) gives $p \equiv 5 \pmod{6}$. The oddness follows from `Nat.Prime.odd_of_ne_two`. This is the tightest residue class constraint available from simple modular arithmetic.
mathContext: $p > 3$ prime and $p \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$ and $p \equiv 1 \pmod{2}$ together give $p \equiv 5 \pmod{6}$ by CRT. The candidates are $5, 11, 17, 23, 29, 35, \ldots$ Of these, not all are SG primes (e.g., 17 is prime but $2(17)+1 = 35 = 5 \times 7$ is not), but all SG primes $> 3$ lie in this progression.
relatedConcepts: Dirichlet's theorem on primes in progressions

title: Safe Prime Properties
content: Two properties of the safe prime $q = 2p+1$: (1) if $p$ is a Sophie Germain prime, then $q$ is prime (this is essentially the definition unwrapped), and (2) $q$ is always odd for $p \geq 1$ (since $2p$ is even, $2p+1$ is odd). These simple lemmas are useful for downstream cryptographic applications.
mathContext: $\text{SafePrime}(p) = 2p + 1$. If $\text{IsSophieGermainPrime}(p)$, then $\text{Nat.Prime}(2p+1)$ by the second component of the SG prime definition. For $p \geq 1$: $(2p+1) \bmod 2 = 1$ since $2p$ is even.
